1.5.3     The method of [80]: Renormalisation, local weights and null structure
In anticipation of the fact that one expects (cf. the discussion in Section 1.4) that the Cauchy horizon
CH+ , although C 0 stable, will generically represent a weak null singularity, the methods introduced in [80]
described in Section 1.4.3 will play an essential role in the proof. For otherwise, the estimates would be
inconsistent with controlling the solution up to CH+ .
    Let us introduce briefly some of the main ideas of [80], directly in the context of Theorem 1.8. The proof
again employs a double null foliation, but we shall denote the coordinates by U and U in place of u and u
to emphasise that these coordinates naturally have finite range [U0 , 0) × [U 0 , 0).
    • Renormalisation. To estimate solutions up to potentially singular null fronts U = 0 and U =
      0 in Theorem 1.8, one must renormalise the Bianchi equations by eliminating the “most singular
      components” α = R(eA , e4 , eB , e4 ), α = R(eA , e3 , eB , e3 ) and replacing the curvature components ρ
      and σ discussed in Section 1.5.1 with
                                        .     1         1                                          1
                                ρ     K = −ρ + χ̂ · χ̂ − /trχ /
                                                             trχ,                  σ       σ̌ = σ + χ̂ ∧ χ̂.
                                              2         4                                          2
        The significance of these quantities K and σ̌ is that K represents the Gaussian curvature of the spheres
        SU,U and σ̌ the curvature of the normal bundle, respectively, and these quantities remain regular up
        to the null boundary. These renormalisations in fact first appeared in [84, 85]. Remarkably, this
        renormalisation respects the structure of Section 1.5.1, i.e. the renormalised system can still be viewed
        as a set of coupled elliptic, transport and hyperbolic equations. Now the elliptic estimates through
        (1.27) appear absolutely essential, not just for the purpose of gaining regularity, but for the system to
        close.26
    • Local weights. Even though the worst behaving components are now removed, the remaining com-
      ponents, e.g. the curvature component β and the shear χ̂ still are not expected to have finite “local”
      energy at a weak null singular front. (This is in contrast to the situation in [84, 85], referred to above,
      where, all Ricci coefficients were locally square integrable.) One can only hope to prove weighted
      estimates with respect to the local “regular” coordinate U , degenerating at U = 0, with weight which
      is integrable at U = 0 when squared. An example of such a weight is
                                                                       1               1
                                                   f (U ) = (−U ) 2 | log(−U )| 2 +δ                                        (1.34)

        appearing in expression (1.21). The finiteness of

                                                           kf (U )χ̂kL2U L2 (SU,U )

        on an outgoing hypersurface U = c is compatible (say in the case of (1.34)) with the pointwise behaviour

                                                   χ̂ ∼ (−U )−1 | log(−U )|−1−2δ .
  26 This is in contrast, for instance, with [31], where elliptic estimates are not used. This in turn was possible because χ̂ could
                                               / 4 χ̂ with α appearing on the right hand side.
be estimated by a transport equation involving ∇


                                                                 28
        Note that this is in turn compatible with the finiteness of the L1 norm

                                                         kχ̂kL1U L2 (SU,U ) ,

        which is to be expected if the metric is to be continuously extendible beyond U = 0.
        For a linear equation like (1.4), such weighted estimates are readily seen to locally propagate. For the
        non-linear Einstein equations (1.1), however, the question of the local propagation of such weighted
        estimates becomes highly non-trivial, dependent on the precise null structure in the nonlinearities.
   • Schematic notation and null structure. In order to describe the above structure, it is useful to
     first introduce a schematic notation.27 One can group (a subset of) the Ricci coefficients into families
     as follows:
                                  ψ ∈ {η, η}, ψH ∈ { /trχ, χ̂}, ψH ∈ { /
                                                                       trχ, χ̂}
        according to their expected singular behaviour. All terms ψH have expected behaviour similar to
        χ̂ (and β) and thus can be estimated either in L1U L2 (S) on outgoing hypersurfaces U = c, or with
        the weight (1.34) in L2U L2 (S). Analogous statements hold for ψH with ingoing hypersurfaces U = c
        replacing outgoing ones. The terms ψ, on the other hand, can be estimated without degeneration.
        Energy identities for β lead in particular to having to estimate spacetime integrals of the form

                                         kf 2 (U )(βψH β + βψH β + βψK)kL1U L1U L1 (S)                                  (1.35)

        All the terms appearing above can be seen to be admissible from the point of view of integrability. In
        contrast, terms like βψH β or βψH β would not have been controllable. It is thus precisely the absence
        of such terms which captures the “null structure” essential for this argument.
    Of course, the story is more complicated, in that the equations need to be sufficiently commuted so
that indeed trilinear terms can be controlled by top order L2 estimates and Sobolev inequalities. We defer
discussion of these issues to the setting of our actual problem in Section 1.5.4 below.

1.5.4     The main estimates
Already in the context of the linear wave equation (1.4) discussed in Section 1.4.1, it is clear that weighted
estimates with respect to the (infinite-range) coordinates u and u are necessary in view of the global aspects
of the problem special to the black hole interior.
    The remarkable fact, central to the present work, is that these two systems of weights, those
introduced in the study of the wave equation as discussed in Section 1.4.1 and those introduced
in [80] as discussed in Section 1.4.3, are in fact compatible, and the null condition is reflected
in both.
    Indeed, we have already seen that the polynomially growing weight in u, coupled with the degenerate
coordinate derivative ∂u and degenerate one-form du, when looked at for fixed u, behaves precisely like
(1.21).
    We outline below the main ideas in adapting the global weighted estimates of (1.4), combined with the
renormalisation of Section 1.5.3, to the global analysis of the Einstein vacuum equations (1.1) in the black
hole interior.

• Transport estimates for Ricci coefficients and wave-type estimates for curvature. In general,
  the Ricci coefficients will be estimated via integrating transport equations while the curvature will be
  estimated from the Bianchi identities. Since the Bianchi identities encode the hyperbolic aspect of
  the Einstein vacuum equations (1.1) expressed in a double null gauge, they are in some sense most
  analogous to the linear wave equation (1.4), their tensorial structure not withstanding. In particular,
  energy estimates with weights related to those described in Section 1.4.1 (see already Section 10)
  would indeed allow one to obtain (1.43) for some of the top order terms displayed in (1.39) and (1.40),
  provided that certain “error terms” can be controlled, which can be classified into various types E1 ,
  E2 , T1 , F2 . (These are defined in Section 8.)
  The analogous estimates for Ricci coefficients are simpler (and precede the treatment of curvature in the
  paper; see already Section 9), following by weighted estimates applied directly to transport equations.
  This again allows for control of all of the lower order estimates for Ricci coefficients displayed in (1.39)
  and (1.40), conditional on being able to recover estimates for error terms. Before turning to the top
  order estimates for the remaining Ricci coefficients let us discuss how some of these error terms are
  estimated.

    The importance of the “null condition” for either long term existence or local regularity issues has been
made clear many times in previous work on the Einstein equations (1.1). The former role is most famously
represented by the monumental proof of the stability of Minkowski space [21], while the latter role can be
seen in the works [84, 80], discussed above, as well as the proof of the bounded L2 curvature conjecture [71].
In this context, it is interesting to remark how in the present work, our weights in u and u capture both
roles of null structure, seamlessly transitioning as u → ∞ from their role in proving sufficiently long-time
existence to their role in ensuring the propagation of low regularity.

1.5.5     Auxiliary issues
Let us briefly comment on certain auxiliary issues in the proof which we have not emphasised so far.



                                                             32
    • Initial data and local existence. An initial data set for (1.1) constitutes a triple (Σ0 , ĝ, k̂) satisfying
      the Einstein constraint equations (see already (4.1)). The first version of our theorem (stated as
      Theorem 4.2) will give a smallness condition expressed solely in terms of the geometric initial data
      ĝ and k̂. Applying well posedness in the smooth category [15], together with ode arguments, we
      will be able to construct locally a double null gauge (1.24) which will be the non-emptiness step of
      the bootstrap argument. We can also globally re-express the initial data in terms of the quantities
      associated to (1.24). This will allow us to give a more precise version of the theorem (stated as
      Theorem 4.27), identifying the smallness condition (1.44), in terms directly related to the quantities
      (1.39), (1.41) appearing in estimates.
    • Sobolev and ellipticity constants. The estimates described in Section 1.5.4 require being able to
      apply the Sobolev inequality to handle lower order terms, and exploiting ellipticity of equations like
      (1.27). This in turn requires quantitative control of various Sobolev constants with respect to the
      induced geometry of the spheres Su,u , and some a priori input on the behaviour of the metric will be
      necessary. The bootstrap assumption (1.42) will suffice for this, and thus bounding these constants
      is in fact the first task of the proof, handled already in Section 5. Note that the conventions related
      to the reduced schematic equations hide many terms estimated by Sobolev, for instance, already in
      writing (1.37).
    • Propagation of higher regularity. As in Christodoulou’s formation of black holes work [20], for
      showing the extendibility of our solution (in the context of step (b) of the bootstrap argument described
      in Section 1.5.2) we will appeal to a local existence result in the C ∞ category, just as we have done
      above to show that the evolution is non-empty.29 On the other hand, the main estimates described in
      Section 1.5.4 close at the finite regularity defined by the quantities (1.39)–(1.41). Thus, to complete
      step (b) of Section 1.5.2, we need to show first the propagation of higher regularity. These estimates are
      typically very straightforward because the equations are linear in the highest order quantities, and one
      only requires the finiteness for given u, not uniform control as u → ∞. Nonetheless, in our problem,
      special care has to be made, however, since, by having renormalised our system as in Section 1.5.3, the
      energies (1.39)–(1.41) no longer control all relevant quantities. This will be the subject of Section 14.

1.5.6    The continuity of the extension
Having shown global existence up to the boundary u = ∞, the last step in the proof of Theorem 1 is to
show that the metric is indeed continuously extendible beyond. This will require certain additional estimates
on the quantity ∇/ 4 log
                      ]  Ω (see already Proposition 16.2). In addition to defining—in complete analogy with
what was already done in the proof of Theorem 1.3 concerning the spherically symmetric toy model of
Section 1.4.2—a rescaled coordinate U = uCH+ , proving continuity now also requires redefining the angular
              A
coordinates (θCH + ) which effectively serves to renormalise the metric coefficient b. We will show in addition

that the spacetime remains close to Kerr in the C 0 norm. This will be the subject of Section 16.

1.5.7    Outline of the paper
We end this guide to the paper with a brief section-by-section account of its contents (referring back to our
discussion above when relevant).
    We begin in Section 2 with a general discussion of the double null gauge (1.24) defined on a suitable
domain U, in particular, putting the Kerr metric in this framework.
    We then present in Section 3 the Einstein vacuum equations (1.1) written in this gauge, moving immedi-
ately to the renormalised form (described above in Section 1.5.3), and introducing the schematic notations ψ,
ψH and ψH . This will allow us in Section 4 to set up the initial value problem with initial data (Σ0 , ĝ, K̂),
giving the two progressively more detailed (cf. the discussion above in Section 1.5.5) statements of Theo-
rem 1, given as Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 4.24, as well as the statement of the main estimates in the
bootstrap region Uuf , Theorem 4.27 (cf. the discussion in Section 1.5.2).
  29 We shall need both local existence for the standard Cauchy problem, for which we quote [15], but also for a characteristic

initial value problem. One could quote [104], but it will in fact be more convenient to appeal to a local existence for the
equations expressed already in the double null gauge, as this ensures that one can obtain a whole neighbourhood of an initial
ingoing hypersurface. See already Section 15.


                                                              33
    Sections 5–13 will concern the proof of Theorem 4.27. We shall use the bootstrap assumption to obtain
in Section 5 preliminary bounds in Uuf on Sobolev constants and ellipticity estimates which will be useful
throughout (cf. Section 1.5.5). This will allow us to derive a general estimate for quantities satisfying
covariant transport equations in Section 6. We then derive in Section 7 the “reduced schematic equations”
for differences, which incorporate L∞ bounds derived by Sobolev that hold in Uuf . Section 8 will define
the error expressions E1 , E2 , T1 , T2 and state Proposition 8.1, which corresponds to the main estimate for
the quantities Nint and Nhyp in terms of these error expressions (cf. the discussion above in Section 1.5.4).
The proof of Proposition 8.1 will then occupy the next three sections: Section 9 will bound the Ricci
coefficients via transport estimates for the null structure equations, Section 10 will bound the curvature via
energy estimates for the Bianchi equations and Section 11 will bound the remaining top order estimates for
Ricci coefficients using elliptic estimates. Finally, the error terms on the right hand side of the estimate of
Proposition 8.1 will be themselves estimated in Section 12, thus completing the proof of the boundedness of
Nint and Nhyp in Uuf , stated as Proposition 12.1 (cf. (1.43)). The bootstrap assumptions will be recovered
in Section 13 (cf. (1.45)), completing the proof of Theorem 4.27.
    With Theorem 4.27, proven, we turn in Section 14 to the propagation of higher regularity discussed
above in Section 1.5.5, which, together with an application of local existence, will allow us in Section 15 to
obtain the global existence part of Theorem 4.24 from Theorem 4.27, stated as Theorem 15.6. This yields
the existence of a solution on U∞ .
    It will remain only to identify the solution (U∞ , g) as the maximal Cauchy development of data, and
show the continuous extendibility of the metric beyond a non-trivial Cauchy horizon (Theorem 16.14);
this will be accomplished in Section 16, completing the proof of Theorem 4.24.
    Although in this paper we do not show that the Cauchy horizon is in any sense generically singular, we
end our paper in Section 17 with a discussion of the compatibility of our estimates with the Cauchy horizon
being a weak null singularity in the sense of [80]. This is given as Theorem 17.1.
    Several computations relating to the Kerr metric in double null gauge are relegated to Appendix A.

1.6    Addendum: the case Λ 6= 0
As is well known, Einstein entertained early on a certain modification [43] of his equations (1.1) by adding
a non-vanishing “cosmological” constant Λ:
                                             1
                                      Ricµν − gµν R + Λgµν = 8πTµν .                                     (1.48)
                                             2
This constant Λ is known observationally to be very small, effectively zero for the scale of astrophysical
black holes which motivate the considerations of this paper. As of the present writing, however, the case of a
small Λ > 0 is favoured on so-called “cosmological” scales where the universe is thought to be approximately
isotropic and homogeneous, and can be described with an energy momentum tensor corresponding to dust.
In contrast, the case Λ < 0 can be related to various speculations in high energy physics, and has received
much recent interest in that context [53].
    In the vacuum, equation (1.48) reduces to

                                                Ricµν = Λgµν .                                           (1.49)

The “trivial” solution of (1.49) with Λ > 0 was first studied in [39] and is known as de Sitter space. The
analogous solution for Λ < 0 is traditionally known as anti-de Sitter space [58]. There is a generalisation
of the Kerr family to (1.49), known as Kerr–de Sitter in the positive case and Kerr–anti de Sitter in the
negative case which contain analogues of “black holes”. These solutions are unfortunately not contained in
the standard elementary textbooks, but one can find a detailed discussion of their geometry in [14].

The cosmological case Λ > 0. In the Kerr–de Sitter case, in addition to an event horizon H+ and Cauchy
horizon CH+ , there is a cosmological horizon C + further partitioning the exterior of the “black hole” into two
subregions. See Figure 20. The region between the event and cosmological horizons is spatially compact and,
in remarkable recent work of Hintz–Vasy [63], this region has been shown to be nonlinearly stable,
as a solution to (1.49), without symmetry assumptions, in the case of parameters sufficiently close to

                                                 CH       CH   +
                                                                            I+
                                                     Σ0
                                                                        C
                                                                        +             H
                                         C+    H +         H+                    C+
                                                                                       +




                                         Σ

                                          Figure 20: The Kerr-de Sitter solution


Schwarzschild–de Sitter. This is an analogue of Conjecture 1 for Λ > 0, restricted to the very slowly rotating
case. In fact, their proof shows the stability of a larger region, and in particular, this yields for all small
perturbations of Schwarzschild–de Sitter the existence of a spacelike hypersurface Σ0 which asymptotes to
Kerr–de Sitter, in analogy with the assumption of our Theorem 1. The rates of convergence are moreover
now exponential , not inverse polynomial, and it is precisely this which makes the global analysis of (1.49)
with Λ > 0 so much more tractable than the Λ = 0 case of astrophysical scales (compare the difficulty of the
proof of stability of Minkowski [21] with the relative ease of that of stability of de Sitter [46]).
    In principle, our Theorem 1 can be put together with [63] to yield the C 0 stability of the region between
the event and Cauchy horizons. It remains to verify that our result allows for the addition of Λ to (1.1),
and to directly relate our decay assumptions on the hypersurface Σ0 or event horizon H+ to the coordinate
set-up of [63].30 In particular, this will disprove unconditionally the analogue of Conjecture 2 for (1.49)
with Λ > 0. For upcoming work on the stability of the “cosmological” region, bounded by C + and I + ,
see [111].
    The story for Λ > 0 has an even more interesting twist, however: We note that heuristic analysis, see [9],
would indicate that the numerology connecting the expected exponential decay rate on the event horizon
and the strength of the blue-shift is such that one expects the metric to be extendible in a W 1,p for a p > 1
depending on the Kerr–de Sitter parameters, with p → ∞ as the parameters approach extremality. In
particular, there is a parameter threshold (close to extremality) beyond which one expects extendibility in
W 1,2 = H 1 . (This is in contrast to the results discussed in Section 1.4.1 for the linear wave equation on
Reissner–Nordström where one has blowup in all W 1,p for p > 1, independently of the parameters Q < M .
Note, however, that in the exactly extremal case |Q| = M considered in [48], one again has extendibility in
W 1,2 !) While [63] does not probe this near-extremal range in view of the restriction to very small a, a recent
result due to Hintz [61] extends [63] to the Einstein–Maxwell system (1.6)–(1.7), proving analogous stability
results for very slowly rotating Kerr–Newmann–de Sitter, in a full neighbourhood of subextremal Reissner–
Nordström–de Sitter. Provided that sufficiently sharp decay rates are obtained, one could then hope to show
that the analogue of Christodoulou’s reformulation of strong cosmic censorship, i.e. Conjecture 3, is false for
Λ > 0. See also [23, 24, 25] for detailed work on this problem in the context of the spherically symmetric
toy model (1.22)–(1.23), when a positive cosmological constant term is added to the left hand side of (1.22).

Instability for Λ < 0? While the case of Λ > 0 is more tractable than that of Λ = 0 in the exterior
of a black hole, the case Λ < 0 is yet harder! Anti de Sitter space itself fails to be globally hyperbolic as
null infinity I is naturally “timelike”, and thus, to obtain well-posed dynamics for (1.49) one must add a
“boundary condition” at I [47]. The most interesting case is that of a reflective boundary condition at I
(see however [65]). In this case, anti de Sitter space itself was conjectured to be unstable, see [30]. This
was first studied numerically in the seminal [5], which moreover related the time-scale of the instability to
resonant interactions understood on the Fourier side. The first proof of AdS instability has recently been
given in the simplest possible setting by Moschidis [89], via an argument entirely physical space-based.
    What allows in principle for instability of AdS at a non-linear level is the lack of decay for the linearised
problem. The situation for black holes is more unclear. The Penrose diagram of Kerr–AdS is depicted in
  30 It is worth noting that, even though the decay assumptions are faster, it does not appear that this leads to a really essential

simplification in the proof of the analogue of our Theorem 1.



                                                                   35
                                                                  +
                                                           CH          CH   +


                                                      I   H   +
                                                                           H+   I

                                                          Σ

                                            Figure 21: The Kerr–AdS solution


Figure 21. Holzegel–Smulevici [66, 67] have shown that while solutions of the linear wave equation on Kerr–
AdS indeed decay, the rate of decay is only logarithmic, and this slow decay is moreover in general sharp.
One scenario is that at the non-linear level, backreaction builds up, and Kerr–AdS shares the unstable fate
of pure AdS, and thus the picture of an event horizon settling down to Kerr–AdS is generically not realised.
If this is the case, then all bets are off regarding the validity of either weak or strong cosmic censorship!
Alternatively, however, the linear picture of slow logarithmic decay could survive in the full non-linear theory,
as is suggested in [40]. The latter situation would mean that the proper setting for understanding black hole
interiors in Λ < 0 requires that we replace the assumption of Theorem 1 or 2 with an assumption of data
on Σ0 or H+ logarithmically approaching that of Kerr–AdS in a suitable sense. Now, it would appear that
such a slow logarithmic decay does not allow for our stability mechanism, for which it seems essential that
one can prove weighted estimates with polynomial weights in u, as in the quantities (1.39)–(1.40). See also
the discussion in [4]. Perversely, could this “worse” event horizon behaviour be sufficient to ensure that the
original C 0 formulation of cosmic censorship (Conjecture 2) becomes true after all for Λ < 0?
    We leave such musings for another occasion!

2     Spacetimes covered by double null foliations
In this section, we will derive the structure equations satisfied by a spacetime (U, g) globally foliated by a
double null foliation intersecting on spheres. We will not require here the metric g to satisfy the Einstein
equations.
    We begin in Section 2.1 with the basic assumptions on the underlying manifold U and metric in explicit
form. We shall then show in Section 2.2 that the geometrical interpretation of these assumptions is
equivalent to the existence of a natural double null foliation; importantly, this allows us to find appropriate
regions of a general spacetime which allow for parametrisation as (U, g). In Section 2.3, we introduce the
Ricci coefficients and curvature components with respect to a natural null frame associated to the double
null foliation, and collect several basic facts about them. Finally, in Section 2.4, we describe how the work
of Pretorius–Israel [103] implies that that Kerr interior can indeed be parametrised as (U, g).

2.1     The general class of spacetimes
We will introduce here the general class of spacetimes (U, g) we will be considering in this paper. The class
of spacetimes is sufficiently general so as to include the Kerr interior and as well as the spacetimes that we
construct31 in Theorem 1.
  31 In fact, it will include both the full spacetimes in Theorem 1, as well as appropriate subsets thereof that we consider in the

context of the bootstrap argument.



                                                                      36
    In Section 2.1.1, we will define the underlying manifold U, followed by the metric and time orientation
in Section 2.1.2. We will define an associated null frame in Section 2.1.3.

2.1.1   The differential structure
Let us denote by u and u the standard Euclidean coordinates on R2 , and let W ⊂ R2 be a connected open
subset, and let S2 denote the standard unit sphere, with local coordinates θA where A = 1, 2. We define the
smooth manifold U = W × S2 .
   We can consider (u, u, θ1 , θ2 ) as local coordinates on U.

2.1.2   The metric and time-orientation
Let γ : W → Γ(T ∗ S2 × T ∗ S2 ) denote a Riemannian metric on S2 , let b : W → Γ(T S2 ) denote a vector field
on S2 , and let Ω : W → Γ(S2 × R) denote a positive function, all depending smoothly on W.
   We can denote the components of b and γ with respect to the local coordinates θA by bA and γAB .
   These choices induce a Lorentzian metric on U defined by:

                     g = −2Ω2 (du ⊗ du + du ⊗ du) + γAB (dθA − bA du) ⊗ (dθB − bB du).                       (2.1)

We time-orient the above by requiring that du and du are future directed. With this choice, (U, g) is a
smooth 4-dimensional spacetime.

2.2     Geometric interpretation and construction of coordinates
We give in this section a geometric interpretation of the above coordinate system and null frame in terms of
the double null foliation that it defines.

2.2.1     The eikonal equation and the double null foliation
Considered as smooth functions u : U → R and u : U → R, the coordinates u and u each satisfy the eikonal
equation
                                    g(Du, Du) = 0, g(Du, Du) = 0.                                   (2.7)
We denote the level sets of u (resp. u) by Hu (resp. H u ). The eikonal equations imply Hu and H u are null
hypersurfaces. We denote
                                             Su,u = Hu ∩ H u .
Note that these are diffeomorphic to S2 and U = ∪(u,u)∈W Su,u .
   Note that the integral flows of L and L respect the foliation Su,u . Moreover, the coordinates (θ1 , θ2 )
obey the condition
                                                LθA = 0.                                            (2.8)

2.2.2     Construction of double null coordinates
We will need the following statement, which constructs locally a double null foliation and a system of double
null coordinates:

Proposition 2.1. Let ` : (a, b) → R2 be a simple curve, Σ = `((a, b)) × S2 and (M, g0 ) be a smooth
Lorentzian 4-manifold. Suppose i : Σ → M is an embedding such that i(Σ) is a spacelike hypersurface.
Prescribe initial data for (u, u, θA ) on Σ as follows:
    • (τ, θA )A=1,2 is a system of local coordinates33 such that τ = `−1 ◦ π (where π : `((a, b)) × S2 → `((a, b))
      is the natural projection map).

    • u Σ is a smooth, strictly increasing function of τ ; u Σ is a smooth strictly decreasing function of τ .
Let y ∈ (a, b). Then there exists an open set W ⊂ R2 with `(y) ∈ W and a metric g in U = W × S2 taking
the form (2.1) such that the following holds:
    • There exists an isometric embedding

                                                         ĩ : (U, g) → (M, g0 ).

    • (u, u, θA ) take their prescribed values on Σ.
    • u and u satisfy (2.7) and θA (for A = 1, 2) is constant along the integral curve of Du.

                                  DL0 L0 = DL0 L0 = 0,        L0 u = L u = 0,      LθA = 0.

2.4     Kerr interior in double null foliation
As we mentioned in the beginning of Section 2.1, the interior of the Kerr spacetime can be put into the form
of the general class of spacetime that we consider. In other words, there exists a global double null foliation
in the Kerr interior. This fact is a consequence of [103]. Detailed discussions of the double null foliation in
the Kerr interior, as well as many calculations and proofs, are deferred to Appendix A. Here, however, we
gather a few facts which will be repeatedly used in the proof of the main theorem.
    Fix M, a ∈ R with 0 < |a| < M . The Kerr interior (MKerr , ga,M ) with mass M and specific angular
momentum a is a spacetime where MKerr = R2 ×S2 and the metric ga,M in the Boyer–Lindquist coordinates
(t,
√ r, θ, φ) takes the form (A.1). Here,   t ∈ R, r ∈ (r− , r+ ), θ ∈ (0, π) and φ ∈ [0, 2π), where r± = M ±
  M 2 − a2 are the roots of ∆ = r2 + a2 − 2M r.
    The Kerr interior (MKerr , ga,M ) admits a global double null foliation so that in an appropriate double
null coordinate system, the metric in MKerr = R2 × S2 takes the form as in the class of spacetimes described
in Section 2.1. More precisely, ga,M can be written as

                ga,M = −2Ω2K (du ⊗ du + du ⊗ du) + (γK )AB (dθA − (bK )A du) ⊗ (dθB − (bK )B du).

where42 ΩK , γK and bK are given in (A.43) (and expressions in (A.43) are functions of (u, u, θ1 , θ2 ) and are
defined implicitly in Sections A.1 and A.4).
    The following are some facts regarding the Kerr metric in this coordinate system that are useful in the
remaining of this paper:

that one can introduce regular coordinates there.

3     Equations in the double null foliation and the schematic nota-
      tion
In this section, we derive consequences of the Einstein vacuum equations under the geometric setup intro-
duced in Section 2. From now on, we consider a spacetime (U, g) (with U = W × S2 and W ⊂ R2 ) where g
takes the form (2.1). Assume that (U, g) satisfies the Einstein vacuum equations (1.1). We will recast (1.1)
as a system for Ricci coefficients and null curvature components (recall the definition from (2.20) and (2.21)
in Section 2.3.2).
    In Section 3.1, we will write down the arising system for Ricci coefficients and null curvature components.
As we have discussed earlier, for most of this paper, the exact form of the terms in the equations will not
be too important. Instead, for most of the nonlinear terms, it suffices to understand the “null structure”
  43 We especially highlight this region since the present paper is exactly concerned with perturbations of the Kerr spacetime

in this region.

hidden in the equations. For this reason, we introduce a schematic notation in Section 3.2 so as to simplify
the exposition and to emphasise the structures of the equations that we need (cf. Sections 1.5.3, 1.5.4 and
[80]). We end the section by writing down the equations in schematic form in Section 3.3.
    Let us already note here that the schematic notation introduced in this section will be further developed
later in Section 7.1, cf. Section 1.5.4.

3.2     Schematic Notation
We introduce a schematic notation for the equations that we consider. We will use the symbol =S to
emphasise that an equation is only to be understood schematically.
    We first introduce schematic expressions for the Ricci coefficients according to the estimates that they
will eventually be shown to obey. More precisely, let

                                     ψ ∈ {η, η},     ψH ∈ { /
                                                           trχ, χ̂},       ψH ∈ { /
                                                                                 trχ, χ̂}.

When writing an equation in the schematic notation, the following conventions will be used:
    • (Numerical constants) We use the convention that the exact constants are kept on the left hand side
      of =S while we do not keep track45 of the constants on the right hand side of =S .
    • (Quantities on left and right hand side) When a schematic quantity, say ψH , appears on the right hand
      side of a schematic equation, one should understand it as summing over all possible ψH ∈ { /       trχ, χ̂}. On
      the other hand, when a schematic quantity, again say ψH , appears on the left hand side, one should
      understand it as representing a fixed ψH ∈ { /trχ, χ̂}. For instance, in (3.8) below, the /∇3 ψH − 2ωψH on
                                                      /3/
      the left hand side is meant to represent either ∇ trχ−2ω /        / 3 χ̂−2ω χ̂ (but not, say, ∇
                                                                 trχ or ∇                           / 3 χ̂−2ω / trχγ).
    • (Contractions with respect to the metric) We will denote by ψψ (or ψψH , etc) an arbitrary contraction
      with respect to the metric γ.
                                          i
    • (Derivatives and products) / ∇ ψ j will be used to denote the sum of all terms which are products of j
                                                       i
      factors, such that each factor takes the form ∇/ k ψ and that the sum of all ik ’s is i, i.e.
                                        i                     i     i        i
                                                    X
                                      ∇ ψ j =S
                                      /                     ∇/ 1 ψ∇
                                                                  / 2 ψ... /
                                                                          ∇ jψ .
                                                            |        {z        }
                                                       i1 +i2 +...+ij =i
                                                                             j factors


    • (The bracket notation) We will use brackets to denote terms with one of the components in the brackets.
      For instance, the notation ψ(ψ, ψH ) denotes the sum of all terms of the form ψψ or ψψH .
  44 Moreover, compared to the renormalisation in [84], this system do not contain the terms / trχ|χ̂|2 and /trχ|χ̂|2 which would
be uncontrollable in the context of this paper. This observation already played an important role in [80].
  45 Obviously, we will use this schematic notation only in situations where the exact constant in front of the term is irrelevant

to the argument.


                                                                47
     • (Extra terms) We will allow in the schematic expression some terms on the right hand side of =S which
       are not present in the original equation46 . This creates no extra problems since in the proof of the
       theorem, we will be bounding all the terms on the right hand side of =S .
     • (Rank of the tensor) When using the schematic notation, we suppress the rank of the tensor involved.
       This will allow us to write schematically the equations for various tensors of different rank in a compact
       manner.
     • (Norm of a schematic quantity) We will often write |ψ|, |ψH |, etc. to denote the norm of a schematic
       quantity, which is understood to be taken with respect to γ.
Remark 3.1 (Differentiating the schematic equations). Note that with the conventions we introduced above,
we can differentiate the schematic equation without knowing precisely the terms on the right hand side of
the schematic equation. For instance, if φ =S φ0 , then it holds that /     ∇φ0 . Similar statements hold for

                                                                   49
4     Statement of main theorem and the construction of the double
      null foliation
In this section, we formulate precisely Theorem 1 of Section 1.3.1. In fact, it will be convenient to state
two versions of the theorem: the first will be given in Section 4.1 as Theorem 4.2, where the notion of
the “expected induced geometry of a dynamical black hole settling down to Kerr on a suitable spacelike
hypersurface Σ0 in the black hole interior” will be given in terms of the geometric data on Σ0 . The second
version will be given in Section 4.7 as Theorem 4.24 in terms of the geometric quantities associated to a double
null foliation (cf. Section 2). The latter version has the additional advantage that it is more in line with
the geometric setup of the proof of the theorem and we can therefore also describe in a quantitative manner
the closeness of the maximal globally hyperbolic future development and the background Kerr solution.
Moreover, we will show that the conditions on the geometric data given in Theorem 4.2 indeed imply the
conditions in Theorem 4.24 for an appropriately defined double null foliation.
    The section will be organised as follows. In Section 4.1, we state Theorem 4.2, which is a formulation
of Theorem 1 in terms of the geometric data on Σ0 . In Section 4.2–Section 4.7, we discuss the formulation of
the main theorem in the double null foliation gauge. More precisely, in Section 4.2, we set up the data for
a double null foliation and a system of double null coordinate system. In Section 4.3, given an appropriate
solution in a double null foliation gauge, we introduce an identification of the spacetime with the background
Kerr spacetime. In Section 4.4, we derive the initial data for the geometric quantities with respect to the
double null foliation gauge. In particular, we prove that given the assumptions on the geometric data in
Theorem 4.2, the data for the differences of the geometric quantities with respect to the double null foliation
gauge are appropriately small. In Section 4.5, we define the initial data energy. In Section 4.6, we
introduce the energies that we will use to control the solution (cf. Section 1.5.4). In Section 4.7, we state
Theorem 4.24, which is our second formulation49 of Theorem 1, and is given in terms of the geometric
quantities in the double null foliation gauge. In Section 4.8, we discuss the main bootstrap assumption
and the main bootstrap theorem (Theorem 4.27).

Remark 4.3. The non-trivial Cauchy horizon CH+ should be understood as a null boundary that one can
attach to the solution in a similar manner as the Cauchy horizon in the Kerr spacetime (cf. Section A.5).
This is in contrast to the “trivial” Cauchy horizon that one can attach to the solution simply because we
restrict our initial data to have an incomplete end. We will give a more descriptive discussion in Remark 4.26
in Section 4.7, after we set up the double null foliation; see also Section 16.
Remark 4.4. The sense in which (M, g) is close to the background Kerr solution will be made precise in
Theorem 4.24 in Section 4.7.

Remark 4.5. It is convenient in this paper to restrict only to the maximal globally hyperbolic future devel-
opment of a subset of Σ0 as indicated in Theorem 4.2. As in the statement of Theorem 4.2, in the remainder
of the paper, we will denote by (M, g) the maximal globally hyperbolic future development only of the subset
Σ0 ∩ {(τ, θ1 , θ2 ) : τ < −uf + CR } ⊂ Σ0 . Nevertheless, when combined with Theorem 3 (which is to appear
in [33]), one sees that this restriction is not necessary, but instead the conclusion of Theorem 4.2 holds for
the entire maximal globally hyperbolic future development of the data on Σ0 .
Remark 4.6. In principle, one can directly construct initial data sets satisfying the constraint equations
that obey the bound (4.2). Nevertheless, we will not pursue this since we will show in [32] that such an initial
data set (Σ0 , ĝ, k̂) indeed arises from solving a characteristic initial value problem starting from a complete
null hypersurface that approaches the event horizon of Kerr spacetimes.

4.3    Identification with Kerr spacetime and the difference quantities
In this subsection, we introduce an identification of an appropriate spacetime arising from (appropriate sub-
sets) of the initial data set (Σ0 , ĝ, k̂) with the background Kerr spacetime (MKerr , ga,M ) (see Appendix A).
This identification relies on the double null coordinates and in particular applies to the solution (Uulocal , g)
that we constructed in Proposition 4.7. Nevertheless, it is convenient to already consider a more general
class of spacetimes.
    For the rest of this subsection, assume we are given a solution (Uuf , g) (see Figure 22) to the Einstein
vacuum equation, where Uuf = Wuf × S2 , and Wuf ⊂ R2 is given by

                                 Wuf = {(u, u) : u + u ≥ CR , u < uf , u < uf }

nates (cf. (4.5)) are as prescribed. On such a spacetime (Uuf , g), we can identify Uuf with the background
Kerr spacetime and compare their geometries. For this purpose, we will use the double null coordinates
(u, u, θ∗ , φ∗ ) on MKerr defined in Section A.4; see also Section 2.4.
    Identification of Uuf with Kerr spacetime. Recall from Section 4.1 that there exists a diffeomorphism

     ground Kerr metric.

both the geometric data and the data (4.5) are achieved on Σ0 = {(u, u) : u > 1, u + u = CR } × S2 . We
can then consider the metric components and the Ricci coefficients with respect to the double null foliation
gauge in Uaux , and restrict them to Σ0 . We define this restriction to be the initial data for the geometric
quantities defined with respect to the double null foliation gauge. It can be easily checked that as long as
(Uaux , g) satisfies the above conditions, the definition of initial data for the geometric quantities defined with
respect to the double null foliation gauge does not depend on the particular choice of (Uaux , g). Moreover,
as we will show below, the initial data for the geometric quantities defined with respect to the double null
foliation gauge can be expressed in terms of the geometric data (Σ0 , ĝ, k̂) alone.
    We will compute these initial data these initial data below. Moreover, we will show that the smallness
assumptions (4.2) and (4.3) for the geometric data translate to smallness conditions for the initial data of
the geometric quantities with respect to the double null foliation gauge.

4.6     Energies for controlling the solution
In this subsection, we define the spacetime energies that we use to control the difference of the geometric
quantities of (Uuf , g) and the background Kerr solution.
    We begin with some preliminaries in Sections 4.6.1 and 4.6.2. After that we define the various Lebesgue
norms (Section 4.6.3) and weights (Section 4.6.4) that we will use to define our energies. Finally, we define
the various energies in Section 4.6.5.

4.6.1   Region of integration
We will always be working in a region (see Figure 22) of the form
                        .          .
                    Uuf = Wuf × S2 = {(u, u) : −uf + CR < −u + CR ≤ u < uf } × S2 .

Here,
   • uf is a parameter quantifying the closeness of the region to timelike infinity. It will be chosen as part
     of the proof of Theorem 4.24 (cf. Theorem 4.2). In the proof, one can therefore view |uf |−1 as a small
     parameter.

   • uf ∈ (−uf + CR , ∞) is arbitrary. We will show that for any choice of uf ∈ (−uf + CR , ∞), under
     appropriate bootstrap assumption, one can control the geometry of the region Uuf . In the context of
     the bootstrap argument (see Sections 1.5.2 and 15), this allows us to conclude that the solution exists
     and remains regular in ∪u∈(−uf +CR ,∞) Uu . Therefore, it is important that (unless explicitly stated
     otherwise) any estimates that we prove are independent of uf .
Without loss of generality (by choosing uf more negative depending on CR otherwise), we will assume from
now on that u ≤ −1 and u ≥ 1 in Uf .

4.6.2   Conventions for integration
When there is no danger of confusion, when integrating
                                                    R      over
                                                           R    the 2-spheres Su,u , we will suppress in our
notation the volume form dV olγ , i.e. we will write Su,u = Su,u dV olγ .

We end this subsection with some remarks on the energies defined above.
Remark 4.18 (Remarks on regularity). We now make some remarks about the number of derivatives used
in the energies above.
   • Our energies control the differences of all the Ricci coefficients up to 3 angular derivatives.
   • Except for the difference K e of the Gauss curvature of the 2-spheres of the double null foliation, the
     curvature components do not explicitly appear in the definition of the energies. This may at the first
     sight seem different from the energies used in [20, 21]. Nevertheless, in the course of the proof, we will
     in fact also control the differences of the renormalised curvature components e β, e
                                                                                       K, ě
                                                                                           σ, β
                                                                                              e in appropriate
     norms up to 2 angular derivatives.
   • Notice however that in the energies above, for the differences of the metric components ge and eb, we in
     general only control up to 3 angular derivatives. In other words, it is only some special combination
     of derivatives of the (differences of the) metric components, namely those which can be written as 3
     angular derivatives of Ricci coefficients, that we control up to 4 derivatives.
Remark 4.19 (Naming of the energies). We name our energies as the integrated energy Nint , hypersurface
energy Nhyp and sphere energy Nsph because
   • for Nint , all the geometric quantities are integrated over all spacetime in the L2u L2u L2 (S) norm;


                                                                               62
    • for Nhyp , many of the geometric quantities are integrated over a constant-u or constant-u null hyper-
      surface (with supremum taken over all such hypersurfaces), i.e. they are controlled in the L∞  2 2
                                                                                                  u Lu L (S)
           ∞ 2 2
      or Lu Lu L (S) norms;
    • for Nsph , many of the geometric quantities are integrated on a 2-sphere Su,u adapted to the double
      null foliation (with supremum taken over all such spheres), i.e. they are controlled in the L∞  ∞ 2
                                                                                                   u Lu L (S)
      norm.
Notice however the following:
    • In the Nhyp energy, it is convenient to have a slightly stronger norm by changing the order of the L2
      and the L∞ norms for the lower order quantities (cf. Remark 4.20 below).
    • In the Nsph energy, in addition to controlling the L∞      ∞ 2
                                                            u Lu L (S) norm of the geometric quantities, we
                                                 i                                                     i

Remark 4.20 (Order of integration in the energies). Let us note that in Nhyp , while there is always one
L2 norm and one L∞ norm in the u, u variable, for the lower derivatives of most of the terms (i.e. up to
two angular derivatives of the Ricci coefficients), the L∞ norm is taken before the L2 norm, while for the
higher derivatives (i.e. third derivatives of the Ricci coefficients), the L∞ norm is taken after the L2 norm.
Recalling Remark 4.15, this means that we control a stronger norm when there are fewer derivatives.58 59

4.7    Statement of main theorem in the double null foliation gauge
We are now ready to state the main theorem:

Theorem 4.24. For every fixed Kerr spacetime with 0 < |a| < M and every δ > 0, CR ∈ (−∞, +∞), there
exists 0 = 0 (a, M, δ, CR ) > 0 and uf = uf (a, M, δ, CR ) ≤ −1 such that the following holds:
    Suppose that for the given geometric initial data (Σ0 , ĝ, k̂) and the initial data for the double null foliation
and double null coordinates defined as in (4.5) in Section 4.2, the initial data energy D obeys

                                                       D ≤ 2                                                  (4.25)

for  ≤ 0 , then the following holds:
   • Let (M, g) be the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of the restriction of the initial data
     on Σ0 ∩ ({τ : τ < −uf + CR } × S2 ) as given by [15]. Then (M, g) can be endowed with a double null
     foliation (u, u) attaining the prescribed initial data for the foliation in Section 4.2 so that it is isometric
                                    .                           .
     to a smooth spacetime (U∞ = W∞ × S2 , g) with W∞ = {(u, u) : u < uf , u + u ≥ CR } and g taking the
     form (2.1).
   • In addition, (U∞ , g) remains close to Kerr spacetime in the sense that

                                                Nint , Nhyp , Nsph ≤ C2 ,                                     (4.26)

      for some C > 0 which depends only on a, M , δ and CR .
   • Moreover, there exists a non-trivial Cauchy horizon CH+ , which is a future null boundary of (U∞ , g),
     across which the spacetime metric extends continuously.
Remark 4.25 (Theorem 4.24 implies Theorem 4.2). In view of Proposition 4.13, Theorem 4.24 implies
Theorem 4.2.

Remark 4.26 (Continuous extension to the Cauchy horizon). In Theorem 4.24, we show that there is a
non-trivial Cauchy horizon across which the spacetime metric extends continuously. (The non-trivial Cauchy
horizon can be thought of as analogous to the Kerr Cauchy horizon. This is in contrast to the null boundary
{u = uf }, which can be thought of as a trivial Cauchy horizon associated to the incompleteness of initial
hypersurface, cf. Section 16.1.) The non-trivial Cauchy horizon can be most easily described in the double
null coordinate system that we are using. We will show that by rescaling u to uCH+ and introducing a new
                         1      2
system of coordinates (θCH + , θCH+ ) on the 2-spheres Su,u (cf. the analogous change of variable in Kerr in

Section A.5.2), one can attach a null boundary CH+ such that the metric extends continuous to the manifold-
                                                                 1       2
with-boundary. Moreover, in the coordinate system (u, uCH+ , θCH    + , θCH+ ), the metric g is in fact close to
                      0
the Kerr metric in C up to and including the Cauchy horizon. See Section 16 for details.
    We note that the first bullet point in Theorem 4.24 will be finally obtained by combining Theorem 15.6
(proven in Section 15) and the fact that (U∞ , g) is indeed the maximal globally hyperbolic future development
of the restriction of the data (proven in Proposition 16.16 in Section 16). The second bullet point in
Theorem 4.24 will be obtained as part of Theorem 15.6 in Section 15. Finally, the third bullet point in
Theorem 4.24 will be obtained in Theorem 16.14 in Section 16. We refer the reader also to Section 16.7,
where the proof of Theorem 4.24 will be completed.

4.8    Main bootstrap assumption
In order to prove the bound (4.26), we will use a bootstrap argument. As above, we assume that we
have a solution (Uuf , g) to the Einstein vacuum equations in a system of double null coordinates with the
prescribed data (see precise statement in Theorem 4.27). Assume that the following bootstrap assumption
holds throughout Uuf :
                                                 Nsph ≤ .                                          (4.27)
Under the bootstrap assumption (4.27), we will prove the bounds on Nint and Nhyp stated in (4.26) in
Sections 5–12. In Section 13, we will then use the estimates on Nhyp to show that (4.27) can be improved
to a bound
                                                Nsph ≤ C2
where C is a constant depending only on a, M , δ and CR and will be chosen later. Thus, for  sufficiently
small depending only on a, M , δ and CR , we have C2 ≤ 2 . This then improves (4.27). We summarise this
discussion in the following theorem, the proof of which will be our goal in Sections 5–13 (see the conclusion
of the proof in Section 13.4).
Theorem 4.27 (Bootstrap theorem). For every fixed Kerr spacetime with 0 < |a| < M and every δ > 0,
CR ∈ (−∞, +∞), there exists 0 = 0 (a, M, δ, CR ) > 0 and uf = uf (a, M, δ, CR ) ≤ −1 such that the following
holds:
            .
   Let (Uuf = Wuf × S2 , g) be a smooth solution to the Einstein vacuum equation, where Wuf ⊂ R2 is given
by Wuf = {(u, u) : u ∈ [−u + CR , uf ), u ∈ [−u + CR , −uf )}, such that

    • the metric g takes the form (2.1),

    • the metric g achieves the prescribed initial data on {(u, u) : u + u = CR } × S2 as in Theorem 4.24.
Assume that (4.25) holds for some  ≤ 0 and that the bootstrap assumption (4.27) holds in Wuf × S2 . Then
the following estimate holds in Wuf × S2 :

                                               Nint , Nhyp , Nsph ≤ C2

for some C > 0 which depends only on a, M , δ and CR .
Remark 4.28 (Comment regarding the smallness constants). Before we proceed, we make a further comment
on the constants in the proof of the theorem. In addition to the size of the initial data , we will use another
smallness parameter N −1 , which appeared60 in the definition of the energies Nint and Nhyp . In the proof
of the theorem, the constants a, M , δ and CR are taken to be given. We will then choose N large and 0
small (in that order) depending on these parameters and show that we can close the bootstrap argument as
described above. In particular, we will always assume that  ≤ 0 ≤ N −1 .
Remark 4.29. Section 5–Section 13 will concern the proof of the bootstrap theorem (Theorem 4.27). In
particular, we will work with a solution (Uuf , g) satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 4.27 and assume that
(4.27) holds without further comments. Moreover, in the proof of the estimates, unless otherwise stated, we
will use61 the notation A . B to denote A ≤ CB for some C > 0 depending only on a, M , δ and
CR . (This dependence of the constants is consistent with that in Theorem 4.27.) In particular, the constants
in . are independent of uf , uf ,  and N .

7     The reduced schematic equations
Recall that we continue to work under the setting described in Remark 4.29.
    In this section, we introduce our notion of reduced schematic equations. These are expressions which
further simplify the schematic equations introduced in Section 3.3 and will be used for the differences of the
geometric quantities and their derivatives. The main additional simplification is that all factors bounded
          ∞ ∞
in L∞u Lu L (S) by a constant depending only on M and a will be suppressed . Reduced schematic
equations will be written with the symbol =RS and a more detailed discussion of the conventions associated
to reduced schematic equations will be given in Section 7.1.
    After introducing the conventions, the main goal of this section is to derive reduced schematic equations
for the angular covariant derivatives (with respect to (Uuf , g)) of the difference of the metric components,
the Ricci coefficients and the renormalised null curvature components.
    In Section 7.2, we will derive the commutation formula for [∇     / 4, /       / 3, /
                                                                           ∇] and [∇    ∇] (Proposition 7.1) and
the formulae for the differences of the connection coefficients /
                                                                ∇− /∇K (Proposition 7.3), ∇ / 3 −( /
                                                                                                  ∇3 )K (Proposi-
tion 7.4) and /
              ∇4 − ( /
                     ∇4 )K (Proposition 7.6). These computations will then allow us to derive general reduced
schematic equations for the difference of the geometric quantities satisfying a / ∇3 equation (Proposition 7.5)
or a ∇/ 4 equation (Proposition 7.7).
    To derive the reduced schematic equations, it is useful to define four types of inhomogeneous terms which
arise in most of the equations for the differences of the geometric quantities. These inhomogeneous terms
will be introduced in Section 7.3. We will denote these terms72 by F1 , F2 , F3 and F4 .
    In the remainder of this section, we then proceed to the derivation of the reduced schematic equations,
showing that indeed only F1 , F2 , F3 and F4 show up as inhomogeneous terms. Section 7.4 will be
dedicated to the reduced schematic equations for γ          ]
                                                    e and log  Ω, eb and their angular covariant derivatives. In
Section 7.5 and Section 7.6, we derive the reduced schematic equations for the Ricci coefficients. Finally,
in Section 7.7, we obtain the reduced schematic equations for the renormalised null curvature components.

7.1     Conventions for the reduced schematic equations
We now formally introduce our notion of reduced schematic equations, already described in Section 1.5.4.
We will use the convention =RS to denote that the “equation” holds only in the reduced schematic sense.
These reduced schematic equations will be equations for the difference quantities, i.e. the e quantities;
see Section 4.3. These include differences of metric components, Ricci coefficients, renormalised curvature
components, quantities in (2.26), and their derivatives.
    The conventions that we will use are as follows:
    • (Conventions from the schematic equations) All the conventions introduced for the schematic equations
      in Section 3.2 will be used for the reduced schematic equations.
    • (Conventions regarding taking differences) All the conventions introduced in Section 4.3 regarding
      taking differences will be used for the reduced schematic equations.
    • (Terms bounded in L∞     ∞ ∞
                            u Lu L (S) are suppressed) On the right hand side of the reduced schematic
      equations, we will use the convention that all factors bounded in L∞       ∞ ∞
                                                                              u Lu L (S) by a constant
      depending only on M and a will not be written. These include terms associated to the geometric
                                                                                           1
      quantities of the background Kerr spacetime, as well as terms which are bounded by  2 in L∞ using
      Corollary 5.6.
    • (Reduced schematic equations cannot be differentiated) We emphasise explicitly that since we suppress
      the terms that are bounded in L∞     ∞ ∞
                                       u Lu L (S) in the reduced schematic equations, one is not allowed
      to differentiate the reduced schematic equations. This stands in contrast to the schematic equations
      introduced in Section 3.2; see Remark 3.1.
    To illustrate the conventions above, we already give an example here. Consider the schematic equation
(3.17). We now take the difference of the /∇3 η equation and the ( /                                 / 3η −
                                                                  ∇3 )K η K equation. First, we have ∇

We briefly comment on these terms. E1 and E2 are error terms which, after bounding appropriate quantities
using the bootstrap assumption (4.27) on Nsph , can be treated essentially by linear estimates. Notice that
E1 contains all of the quantities ψeH , ψeH , ψ,        e while E2 only contains the subset ψ,
                                              e ge, eb, K                                   e ge, K.
                                                                                                  e Moreover, for
the quantities that appear in both E1 and E2 , they show up in E2 with a worse weight. On the other hand,
the terms T1 and T2 cannot be treated by linear estimates alone. It will be important that we can capture
the full trilinear structure of these terms.

                                                                                    100
Remark 8.2 (Bulk terms with a good sign and the estimates for Nint ). As we already discussed in Sec-
tion 1.5.4, an important aspect of our proof is that while proving the transport and energy estimates, some
bulks terms (i.e. those that are integrated over spacetime) with a good sign can be generated. These terms
give us the desired bounds for Nint .
    There are two ways that these terms are generated. Some of these good bulk terms are generated because
of the $N weights that we have put in the energies. Note that these terms are moreover proportional to N
(cf. (8.2) in the statement of Proposition 8.1). Hence, by choosing N to be large, these terms are useful in
handling many error terms.
    However, not all of the good bulk terms are generated in this way by the $ weight. In fact, the bulk terms
               e with only ΩK weights in Nint estimates84 are not generated by the $N weights. Instead, the
for ge, ψe and K
signs of these terms, which fortunately work in our favour in this case, are dictated by the geometry of the
interior of Kerr solution.
    Finally, note that this type of bulk terms with a good sign is already useful in establishing energy estimates
for the linear scalar wave equation (1.4); see Section 1.4.1.


9     Estimates for the integrated energies via transport equations
Recall that we continue to work under the setting described in Remark 4.29.
    From this section to Section 11, our goal is to bound the integrated energy Nint and the hypersurface
energy Nhyp for the metric components, Ricci coefficients and the renormalised null curvature components
and to prove Proposition 8.1. In this section, we begin with estimating a subset of the terms in Nint and
Nhyp which have the property that their bounds can be proved using transport equations alone. This section
is organised as follows. We begin with some preliminary pointwise estimates for the difference of the metric
components and their derivatives (Section 9.1).We then prove the main estimates of this section, including
the bounds for the difference of the metric components up to their third angular covariant derivatives
(Section 9.2) and the difference of the Ricci coefficients up to their second angular covariant derivatives85
(Section 9.3). In Section 9.3, we also prove some estimates for the quantities (2.26) and their angular
covariant derivatives. (These estimates will be used later in Section 11.)
    As we will see below, given the reduced schematic equations in Section 7 and the general propositions for
deriving estimates from transport equations in Section 6, the estimate that we derive in this section simply
follows from comparing the inhomogeneous terms F1 , F2 , F3 , F4 with the error terms E1 , E2 , T1 , T2 .

10       Energy estimates for the null curvature components
Recall that we continue to work under the setting described in Remark 4.29.
    In this section, we derive the energy estimates for the second angular covariant derivatives of the difference
of the renormalised null curvature components β, K, σ̌, β.
    The derivation of the energy estimates in this section is similar to that for the estimates in the previous
section, except that the equations for β, K, σ̌, β form a system of hyperbolic equations instead of transport
equations. For this reason, we need an extra integration by parts on the 2-spheres Su,u to avoid the loss of
derivatives. To this end, we recall the following standard integration by parts formula on Su,u , which can
be proved by a direct computation:
Proposition 10.1. Given S-tangent tensor fields (1) φ and (2) φ with ranks r and r − 1 respectively,
           Z                                        Z                                      
                  (1) A1 A2 ...Ar /                         A
                     φ           ∇Ar (2) φA1 ...Ar−1 +    ∇ r (1) φA1 A2 ...Ar (2) φA1 ...Ar−1 = 0.
                                                          /
                   Su,u                                           Su,u

    There are two main energy estimates that will be proven in this section. Before we prove these energy
estimates, we first make some general comments on how we apply (4.27) and Sobolev embedding to control
the nonlinear terms in Section 10.1. This discussion will also be relevant in later sections. Then, the
                2e    2 e       2                                                        2e   2 e       2

11       Elliptic estimates
Recall that we continue to work under the setting described in Remark 4.29.
    In this section, we obtain the bounds for the third angular derivatives of the difference of the Ricci
                                                                 3      3      3f       3e    3f        3e          3
coefficients, i.e. we will prove Nhyp and Nint estimates for ∇  / ηe, ∇
                                                                      / η    / trχ,
                                                                          e, ∇   / ∇  / χ̂, / trχ,
                                                                                            ∇   / ∇   / χ̂   and ∇ / ωe.
These estimates will be derived using a combination of transport estimates and elliptic estimates. More
                                                                        2      2      3f      3f
precisely, we first use transport equations to derive estimates for ∇ / µ    / e
                                                                          e, ∇   µ, /
                                                                                    ∇ /trχ, /
                                                                                            ∇ /trχ and /   ∇/ωe. (Some
of these transport estimates were already derived in Section 9.3.) These quantities, while being top order in
terms of derivatives, are chosen so that the transport equations they obey do not contain terms with three
derivatives of the curvature components90 . We will then use the elliptic structure that was understood in
[20, 21] hidden in the equations for the Ricci coefficients, and apply the elliptic estimates in Propositions 5.7
and 5.8 to prove all the top order estimates for the Ricci coefficients.
                                                                    3         3
    This section will be organised as follows: The estimates for ∇/ ηe and / ∇ ηe will be proved in Section 11.1;
                       3f         3e                                                           3         3           3
the estimates for /  ∇ /        / χ̂ will be proved in Section 11.2; the estimates for /
                        trχ and ∇                                                           ∇ /f trχ, ∇/ e χ̂ and /∇ ω e
will be proved in Section 11.3.
    In order to close our elliptic estimates in Section 11.3, we will also need to obtain some additional
estimates for ge and their angular covariant derivatives (Proposition 11.12). These will in turn also give the
           i
bounds ∇ / η e for i ≤ 2 in L∞  2 2
                             u Lu L (S) (Proposition 11.13). With all of these estimates, we will thus conclude
the proof of Proposition 8.1 in Section 11.4.

11.4      Proof of Proposition 8.1
We have now controlled the third angular covariant derivatives of all the differences of Ricci coefficients.
Together with the estimates obtained in the previous sections, we have therefore controlled Nint and Nhyp
(see (4.22) and (4.23)). In particular, we conclude the proof of Proposition 8.1:
Proof of Proposition 8.1. Proposition 8.1 is a consequence of the combination of Propositions 9.3, 9.5, 9.6,
9.7, 9.8, 9.10, 9.11, 9.13, 10.2, 10.3, 11.2, 11.6, 11.12, 11.13 and 11.15.


12      Controlling the error terms
Recall that we continue to work under the setting described in Remark 4.29.
    By Proposition 8.1, we have obtained estimates for the metric components, the Ricci coefficients and the
curvature components in the hypersurface energy Nhyp and the integrated energy Nint in terms of the error
terms E1 , E2 , T1 and T2 . In this section, we will prove the opposite bounds: we will show that the error
terms E1 , E2 , T1 and T2 can be controlled by the Nhyp energy and the Nint energy. Moreover, by choosing
N sufficiently large and 0 (and hence ) sufficiently small, we can show that there is a smallness constant in
the estimates such that we can indeed derive the boundedness of Nhyp and Nint . The following proposition
is the main goal of this section, the proof of which will be achieved in Section 12.4:
Proposition 12.1. For N sufficiently large and 0 sufficiently small depending on M , a, δ and CR , we have

                                                         Nhyp + Nint . 2 ,

whenever  ≤ 0 where the implicit constant depends only on M , a, δ and CR .
    After we prove this proposition in Section 12.4, we will then fix the parameter N .
    The section is organised as follows. In Section 12.1, we define the energies Nint,1 , Nint,2 and Nhyp,1 ,
which contain subsets of terms in Nint and Nhyp , and will be used to estimate the error terms. We then
briefly explain the strategy used to control the error terms. In Section 12.2, we bound the E1 , E2 error
terms; in Section 12.3, we bound the T1 , T2 error terms. Finally, in Section 12.4, we put together these
estimates to conclude the proof of Proposition 12.1.

for many of the lower order terms, we can take L∞ before taking L2 . To exploit this, we will often use
Remark 4.15 without explicit comment.

parameter N .

14      Propagation of higher regularity
After having proven Theorem 4.27 in the last section, we return to the proof of Theorem 4.24. Our next
goal will be to prove Theorem 15.6 in which we establish the existence of a solution (U∞ , g). Meanwhile, we
first have to propagate higher regularity (cf. Section 1.5.5). This is achieved in the present section.
    More precisely, we use the estimates derived in Theorem 4.27 to propagate estimates for any higher
derivatives of the Ricci coefficients and renormalised curvature components. As is standard, since we have
already closed the lower order estimates, the higher order estimates are essentially linear in the unknown.
These higher order terms can therefore be controlled using a Grönwall-type argument. The only slightly
subtle issue is that because we are only controlling the renormalised curvature components (β, K, σ̌, β), it is
not a priori clear that this is sufficient to bound, say, all the spacetime curvature components. Nonetheless, we
will show that restricting to in a finite u region, precisely because the Ricci coefficients and the renormalised
curvature components form a closed system of equations, we can differentiate that system to obtain all higher
order estimates. A similar propagation of higher regularity argument can be found in [84].
    The setting of this section is as follows. We will consider the domain Uuf = Wuf × S2 , where, as before,
Wuf is the closed-to-the-past, open-to-the-future triangular domain in the (u, u)-plane given by

                         Wuf = {(u, u) : u ∈ [−u + CR , uf ), u ∈ [−u + CR , uf )} ⊂ R2 .                 (14.1)
From now on until the end of this section, assume that we have a smooth solution to the Einstein vacuum
equations (1.1) in Uuf in the double null coordinate system, which achieves the given data in Theorem 4.24
and assume that the estimate (4.27) holds. By Theorem 4.27, this implies the estimate Nint , Nhyp , Nsph . 2 .
    Our goal in this section is to prove that all derivatives of ψ, ψH , ψH , ω and K are bounded in Uuf .
Of course all the higher derivative estimates may degenerate as uf → ∞, which is why we control the
renormalised quantities instead in the first place. Therefore, unlike in the previous sections, all estimates
in this section are allowed to depend on uf , in addition to M , a, δ and CR . We will emphasise
this by adding a subscript uf in all the constants. (These constants are allowed to differ from line to
line.) These estimates, though they degenerate as uf → ∞, will be sufficient for showing that the metric
remains smooth in Uuf = Wuf × S2 and extends to a smooth metric on the manifold-with-corner Wuf × S2
(cf. Proposition 14.7). We will then use this fact to conclude the bootstrap argument in the next section.
    We begin with the following simple calculus lemma, which can be thought of as a 2-dimensional analogue
of the Grönwall’s inequality:

Proposition 14.7. In the coordinate system defined above, the metric extends smoothly to the manifold-
with-corner Wuf × S2 , where the closure is to be understood as the closure in R2 .

Proof. Define the extension in the natural manner: For any p ∈ (∂Wuf \ Wuf ) × S2 , take a sequence
pn → p with pn ∈ Wuf × S2 and define γAB (p) = limn→∞ γAB (pn ), bA (p) = limn→∞ bA (pn ), log Ω(p) =
limn→∞ log Ω(pn ).
   That this is well-defined, independent of the choice of the sequence pn and that the extension is a smooth
metric on Wuf × S2 all follow from the uniform bounds for γAB , bA and log Ω and their derivatives proven
in Proposition 14.6.


15     Completion of the bootstrap argument
We now carry out the bootstrap argument and complete the proof (cf. Theorem 15.6) of
   • the existence of a smooth solution to the Einstein vacuum equations (1.1) in the double null foliation
     gauge with prescribed initial data (i.e. both the geometric initial data and initial data for the double
     null gauge as in Section 4.2) in U∞ = {(u, u) : u ∈ [−u + CR , uf ), u ∈ [−u + CR , ∞)} × S2 , and

   • the estimate (4.26) holds everywhere in U∞
as stated in Theorem 4.24. (The statement on the continuous extendibility of the metric to the Cauchy
horizon will be proven in Section 16; see Theorem 16.14.)
   Define I ⊂ (−uf + CR , ∞) to be the set of all uc ∈ (−uf + CR , ∞) ⊂ R such that the following holds for
W = Wuc = {(u, u) : u ∈ [−u + CR , uc ), u ∈ [−u + CR , uf )} ⊂ R2 :

(A) There is a smooth solution g on U = W × S2 satisfying Ric(g) = 0 in a system of double null coordinates
    (cf. Sections 2 and 3.1) achieving the geometric initial data (ĝ, k̂) and the initial data for the double
    null gauge as in Section 4.2.
(B) The estimate (4.26) holds on U = W × S2 .

Our goal is to show that I = (−uf + CR , ∞). Using connectedness of (−uf + CR , ∞), this will be achieved
in Propositions 15.1, 15.5, 15.2 and Theorem 15.6 below.
Proposition 15.1. I is non-empty.
                                                                                        .
Proof. By Proposition 4.7, there exists ulocal > −uf + CR such that for Wulocal = {(u, u) : u + u ≥ CR , u <
                              .
uf , u < ulocal } and Uulocal = Wulocal × S2 , there is a solution (Uulocal , g) to the Einstein vacuum equations

double null foliation and double null coordinates.
    Moreover, by (4.25), D ≤ 2 . Hence, by continuity, and taking ulocal closer to −uf + CR if necessary, the
estimate (4.26) holds for (Ulocal , g)
    It then follows that ulocal ∈ I. In particular, I is non-empty.

                                     .

We now take W = WCauchy ∪Wchar and combine the solution in WCauchy ×S2 with the solution in Wchar ×S2 .
Since the solution is smooth in WCauchy × S2 and Wchar × S 2 , the solution in W × S2 is piecewise smooth.
Moreover, the solution in W × S2 is everywhere continuous and is smooth up to H on each side. Finally,
it remains to note that in the double null foliation gauge, the derivatives of the metric to transversal107 to
H are determined by the Einstein vacuum equation (1.1), and the limits from each side of H must agree.
Therefore, the solution in W × S2 is smooth, and we have obtained the desired conclusion.
107 Note that this is true for all higher order transversal derivatives.

Proposition 15.5. Choosing 0 smaller if necessary, I is open.
Proof. Suppose uc ∈ I.
    By Proposition 14.7, the metric can be extended smoothly to Wuc × S2 . Therefore, by Lemma 15.4, we
can extend the solution by solving the mixed characteristic Cauchy initial value problem to obtain a smooth
solution in the double null foliation gauge in Wuc +u × S2 for some u > 0.
    Finally, by definition of I, the estimate (4.26) holds in Wuc × S2 . By continuity, this implies that the
estimate (4.26) holds in Wuc × S2 . In particular, since (4.26) is a strictly stronger estimate than (4.27) for
0 (and hence ) sufficiently small, by continuity, every point in Wuc × S2 has an open neighbourhood such
that the bootstrap assumption (4.27) holds. By compactness of Wuc × S2 , this implies that there is some
u > uc such that Wu satisfies (A) and (4.27). Applying Theorem 4.27, it follows that (4.26), and therefore
(B), holds in Wu .
   By the connectedness of (−uf + CR , ∞), Propositions 15.1, 15.2 and 15.5 imply that I = (−uf + CR , ∞).
                                                                                                        .
This then implies that the conditions (A) and (B) stated in the beginning of the section hold for W∞ =
