16       Continuity of the metric up to the Cauchy horizon
In this section, we show that a non-trivial Cauchy horizon CH+ can be attached to (U∞ , g) (cf. Theorem 15.6)
and moreover that the metric can be extended continuously to the Cauchy horizon. This will be achieved in
Theorem 16.14 in Section 16.5. This will be the main remaining ingredient which we use to complete the
proof of Theorem 4.24 in Section 16.7.
    For the purpose of showing the continuous extendibility of the metric, it is important to have precise
estimates for various geometric quantities u → ∞. For this reason, in this section, all the implicit
constants in . are only allowed to depend only on M , a, δ and CR , and all the estimates are
required to hold uniformly in U∞ .
    This section is organised as follows. In Section 16.1, we define the Cauchy horizon CH+ by attaching
an appropriate boundary in the (u, uCH+ , θ1 , θ2 ) coordinate system as in the Kerr case (see Section A.5). In
Section 16.2, we prove some auxiliary estimates for /   ∇4 log
                                                            ]  Ω. Already at this point we show in Section 16.3
that some geometric quantities can be extended continuously to CH+ . In Section 16.4, we introduce a
                                        1       2
different coordinate system (u, uCH+ , θCH + , θCH+ ) and prove estimates related to the change of variable. We

then prove in Section 16.5 that in this new coordinate system, the metric extends continuously to CH+
(Theorem 16.14). In Section 16.6, we prove that in this new coordinate system, the metric is moreover
close to the Kerr metric (in an appropriate coordinate system) in C 0 . We end this section by concluding the
proof of Theorem 4.24 in Section 16.7.

16.1     The Cauchy horizon CH+
16.1.1    Definition of uCH+ and the Cauchy horizon
Let (U∞ , g) be as in Theorem 15.6. Notice that according to Proposition 14.7, the metric extends smoothly
up to {u = uf } (or more precisely, up to W∞ × S2 , where the closure is to be understood with respect to the


                                                     165
natural topology of the (u, u)-plane.) The boundary {u = uf } can be viewed as a “trivial” Cauchy horizon,
whose existence is simply associated to the incompleteness of the initial hypersurface Σ0 ∩ {τ > −uf + CR }
(as τ → −uf + CR ). On the other hand, we will define a non-trivial Cauchy horizon, which can be thought
of as analogous to the Kerr Cauchy horizon. From now on, when we refer to the Cauchy horizon, we will be
referring to this non-trivial Cauchy horizon.
    We define the Cauchy horizon CH+ as follows: Introduce the function uCH+ as in the Kerr case in
Section A.5, i.e. uCH+ (u) is a smooth and strictly increasing function of u, which agrees with u for u ≤ −1,
satisfies uCH+ → 0 as u → ∞ and moreover there exists u− ≥ −1 such that
                                                                r   −r
                                                                    −
                                                 duCH+ (u)    − +
                                                                2   2 u
                                                           = e r− +a for u ≥ u− .                                             (16.1)
                                                    du

Given u as before, uCH+ as above, and (θ1 , θ2 ) a system of local coordinates on the spheres with initial data
(4.5) and satisfying LθA = 0, attach the boundary CH+ to the set {(u, u, θ1 , θ2 ) : u < uf , uCH+ < 0} where
CH+ = (−∞, uf ) × {uCH+ = 0} × S2 .
    Given the above, we then consider U∞ ∪CH+ as a manifold-with-boundary. Defining moreover Suf ,CH+ =
{(u, u, θ1 , θ2 ) : u = uf , uCH+ = 0} in the coordinate system, we can consider U∞ ∪ {u = uf } ∪ CH+ ∪ Suf ,CH+
as a manifold-with-corner.

16.1.2    Differential structures on U∞ ∪ CH+
We define two differential structures on U∞ ∪CH+ . The first one is defined as the natural differential structure
associated to the (u, uCH+ , θ1 , θ2 ) coordinate system. The second one is the natural differential structure
                          1       2
associated to (u, uCH+ , θCH + , θCH+ ), which is a new coordinate system that we will define (see Section 16.4).

with respect to the latter differential structure.108 We make two important remarks regarding the difference

16.3     Preliminary continuity estimates
In this subsection, our goal (see Lemma 16.6 below) will be to show that some of the geometric quantities,
which are originally defined on U∞ can be extended continuously to CH+ (with respect to the differential
structure corresponding to (u, uCH+ , θ1 , θ2 ) coordinate system).
    We begin with an improvement (see Corollary 16.5) of the Sobolev inequality in Proposition 5.5, which
also gives a bound in the Hölder space in addition to a bound in L∞ . Such an improved inequality is known
as Morrey’s inequality. We first define the C α norm:
Definition 16.3. Let S be a closed smooth 2-manifold, γ be a continuous Riemannian metric on S and
α ∈ (0, 1). Then given a function ξ : S → R, we define the C α -norm by

                                              .      |ξ(x) − ξ(y)|γ(x)
                                 kξkC α (S,γ) = sup                  α + kξkL∞ (S,γ) ,
                                                x,y∈S (distγ (x, y))

where distγ (x, y) is the distance between the points x and y induced by the Riemannian metric γ.
   We will use the following standard Morrey’s inequality on smooth Riemannian manifolds. For the pur-
poses of our application, we also note that the constant in Morrey’s inequality can be uniformly controlled
under sufficiently small C 0 perturbations of the metric:
Proposition 16.4. For any closed smooth 2-manifold S with a smooth Riemannian metric γ and 0 < α < 12 ,
the following estimate holds for all functions ξ : S → R with a constant C = C(γ, α) > 0 depending on the
metric γ:                                               X i

with a constant C depending on γ1 and α.

16.6      C 0 -closeness to the Kerr metric
In this subsection, we show that the metric we have constructed in Theorem 16.14 is in fact C 0 -close to the
background Kerr metric, all the way up to and including the Cauchy horizon CH+ . Let us note that we
have already proven that (as in the statement of Theorem 4.24) the spacetime is close to Kerr in the sense
of (4.26). On the other hand, one may be interested in a closeness statement in terms of the C 0 norm of
the metric component, in a coordinate system for which the metric extends continuously up to the Cauchy
horizon. For this purpose, we consider the metric in the coordinate system as in Theorem 16.14, with metric
components given in (16.59) and (16.60).
     In order to compare this metric with Kerr, we will need to use a different identification of (U∞ ∪ CH+ , g)
with (MKerr ∪ CH+ , ga,M ). For this purpose, recall the various coordinate systems on the 2-spheres θ(i)           A
                                                                                                                      ,
 A               A
θ(i),CH+ and θ(i),CH+ ,K (see in particular Corollary 16.9 and (16.9)). Now, instead of identifying the two
                                                  1    2
spacetimes via identifying the (u, uCH+ , θ(i)      , θ(i) ) coordinates (as we did up to this point), we identify the
                    1         2                        +                   1            2                        +

16.7       Conclusion of the proof of Theorem 4.24
We are now ready to conclude the proof of Theorem 4.24. Given Theorems 15.6 and 16.14, it remains to
check that (U∞ , g) is indeed the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of Σ0 ∩ {τ > −uf + CR }:
Proposition 16.16. The solution (U∞ , g) is the maximal globally hyperbolic future development of Σ0 ∩{τ >
−uf + CR }.
Proof. (U∞ , g) is by definition a future development. Hence, it suffices to prove maximality124 . Suppose
not, i.e. there exists a proper globally hyperbolic future extension (M, g) of (U∞ , g). Consider a (smooth)
future-directed causal curve Γ which passes from (U∞ , g) to (M, g) such that Γ U∞ is a future-directed
inextendible causal curve in (U∞ , g). Since Γ U∞ is inextendible, it follows that either supΓ u = uf or
supΓ u = ∞ (otherwise Γ U∞ is contained in a compact subset of Uuf , which contradicts inextendibility).
In particular, there exists a sequence of points {qn }∞                                            +
                                                      n=1 ⊂ Uuf and a point q ∈ ∂U∞ with qn+1 ∈ J (qn ) and
                                                                  −
qn → q such that either u(qn ) → uf or u(qn ) → ∞. However, J (q) ∩ (Σ0 ∩ {τ > −uf + CR }) (as a subset
of M) is then non-compact, contradicting global hyperbolicity.
Proof of Theorem 4.24. This follows from Theorems 15.6 and 16.14 and Proposition 16.16.


17       Relation with weak null singularities
In this final section, we discuss the relation between the spacetimes that we have constructed in Theorem 1
and the spacetimes with essential weak null singularities constructed in [80]. Recall from the discussion in
the introduction (see Conjecture 3) that conjecturally a generic subclass of the class of initial data considered
in Theorem 1 lead to an essential weak null singularity. While we have not proved that any of the spacetimes
we constructed are actually singular, we show in this section that the estimates that we have proven in this
paper for the spacetime metric are consistent with this expectation. In particular, we show that the upper
bounds that we have obtained in the course of the proof of Theorem 1 are comparable to those assumed
in [80] (see Theorem 17.1).

    We will later define the event horizon H+ and the Cauchy horizon CH+ so that MKerr = MKerr ∪ H+ ∪

    We briefly outline the organisation of this section. Our main goal is to introduce the double null foliation
in MKerr so that we can use the geometric setup introduced in Section 2. In Section A.1, we introduce
the Pretorius–Israel coordinate system (t, r∗ , θ∗ , φ) from [103]. In Section A.2 and Section A.3, we then
prove estimates regarding the change of variable (t, r, θ, φ) 7→ (t, r∗ , θ∗ , φ). Using this, we then introduce
in Section A.4 a double null coordinate system (u, u, θ∗ , φ∗ ) so that the metric ga,M takes the form as in
Section 2.1.1. In Section A.5, we introduce the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon, which can be viewed
as boundaries of MKerr . In Section A.6, we derive estimates for the Ricci coefficients. In Section A.7, we
then obtain bounds for the renormalised null curvature components. Finally, in Section A.8, we consider
spacelike hypersurfaces in MKerr .

A.2     Basic estimates on r∗ and θ∗
We now move on to obtaining estimates on r∗ , θ∗ and their derivatives. In particular, we will also prove that
θ∗ is well-defined via the relation (A.3). Our goal is to show that while r∗ and θ∗ are only defined implicitly,
we can nonetheless obtain strong enough estimates on r∗ , θ∗ and their derivatives for the purpose of the
proof of our main theorem. In view of (A.4), it suffices to consider θ ∈ (0, π2 ). We will therefore make this
assumption in the remainder of this subsection.
    Before we proceed, we introduce a convention: in what follows, we will use the notation A . B
to denote the statement that A ≤ CB for some constant C > 0. Unless otherwise stated, this
constant will only be allowed to depend on M and a. (Note in particular that we also allow this
convention to be used when A, B are both negative.)

A.5     The event horizon and the Cauchy horizon
Equipped with the definitions of the null coordinate functions u and u, we now define in this section the
event horizon H+ and the Cauchy horizon CH+ . In particular, we will define MKerr = MKerr ∪ H+ ∪ CH+
to be a manifold-with-corner.

A.5.1    Another system of double null coordinates for r close to r+
To define the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon, we introduce two more systems of double null coordi-
nates. First, define uH+ , uH+ and φ∗,H+ as follows
   • Define uH+ : R → (0, ∞) to be a smooth and strictly increasing function satisfying

         – uH+ (u) = u for u ≥ 1,
         – uH+ (u) → 0 as u → −∞, and

A.5.3    Definition of the event horizon
After the above preliminaries, we now define the event horizon. Using the coordinate chart (uH+ , uH+ , θ∗ , φ∗,H+ )
defined in Section A.5.1, attach the boundary H+ = H1+ ∪ H2+ ∪ S2H+ where H1+ = {uH+ = 0} × (0, ∞) × S2 ,
H2+ = (0, ∞) × {uH+ = 0} × S2 and S2H+ be the 2-sphere with (uH+ , uH+ ) = (0, 0), which is a common
boundary to both H1+ and H2+ . We will call H+ the event horizon.
    It can be checked that that ga,M extends to a smooth Lorentzian metric on MKerr ∪ H+ .

A.5.4    Definition of the Cauchy horizon
The Cauchy horizon CH+ is defined in a similar manner. Using the coordinate chart (uCH+ , uCH+ , θ∗ , φ∗,CH+ )
defined in Section A.5.2, attach the boundary CH+ = CH1+ ∪ CH2+ ∪ S2CH+ where CH1+ = (−∞, 0) × {uCH+ =
0} × S2 , CH2+ = {uCH+ = 0} × (−∞, 0) × S2 and S2CH+ be the 2-sphere with (uCH+ , uCH+ ) = (0, 0) which is
a common boundary to both CH1+ and CH2+ . We will call CH+ the Cauchy horizon.
    As in Section A.5.3, it can be checked that the Kerr metric on MKerr extends to a smooth Lorentzian
metric on MKerr ∪ CH+ .

A.5.5    MKerr as a manifold-with-corner
Combining all the discussions above, we now define MKerr = MKerr ∪ H+ ∪ CH+ as a manifold-with-corner.
Moreover, the Kerr metric on MKerr extends smoothly to MKerr .

    In the next proposition, we will obtain a uniform upper bound on the isoperimetric constant on Su,u .
Before we proceed, we recall the definition of the isoperimetric constant. Given a Riemannian 2-surface
(S, γ), we define the isoperimetric constant I(S, γ) by
                                                        min{Area(U ), Area(U c )}
                                   I(S, γ) = sup                                  .
                                               U           (Perimeter(∂U ))2
                                             ∂U ∈C 1

The importance of the isoperimetric constant in the context of this paper lies in the fact that it is intimately
tied to the constants in the Sobolev embedding theorems, c.f. Propositions 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 5.5. We now state
the bound we have for the isoperimetric constant on the Kerr spacetime:
Proposition A.22. There exists a constant IK > 0 (depending on M and a) such that

                                              sup I(Su,u , γK ) ≤ IK .
                                              u,u

Proof. First, notice that given two 2-spheres Su1 ,u1 and Su2 ,u2 such that u1 +u1 = u2 +u2 = r∗ , by identifying
the value of the coordinate functions θ∗ and φ∗ on Su1 ,u1 and Su2 ,u2 , it is easy to see that Su1 ,u1 and Su2 ,u2
are in fact isometric. In particular, the isoperimetric constant is only a function of the r∗ value associated
to the 2-sphere. Second, since the isoperimetric constant is continuous in r∗ , it is uniformly bounded for
r∗ ∈ K, where K is any fixed compact set of R. It therefore suffices to show that I(Su,u , γK ) does not go to
infinity as r∗ → ±∞, which is obvious since γK has a smooth limit as r∗ → ∞ or r∗ → −∞.

A.8       Spacelike hypersurfaces in MKerr

with that of Kerr, we briefly discuss in this subsection the induced metric and second fundamental form on
spacelike hypersurfaces in MKerr . We will moreover do so in a coordinate system that is easy to compare
with the double null coordinate system that we discussed earlier.
